transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Karen Brooks (Northfield - Head of Platform), Amit Patel (CTO), Lena Zhao (Security)

Summary: quick discovery focused on Dedicated capacity: reserved GPUs, isolation/VPC requirements, burst/bursting policy, scaling expectations and SLAs. Customer concerned about throughput for peak trading hours, data residency and audit logs. Next steps agreed: pricing, benchmark plan, security deep-dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sam from Redwood, I'll hand off to Diego in a sec to get into the technical bits but quick run through agenda, ok?
[00:12] Karen: Yep, thanks Sam. We've got about an hour, Amit and Lena are on for the infra and security questions.
[00:18] Diego: Cool, hi all, SE Diego. We'll cover dedicated capacity, size recommendations, how we handle isolation, burst mechanisms and what scaling looks like operationally. 
[00:30] Amit: Great. For context we run batch and real-time inference; real-time is for client-facing support flows plus a high frequency reconciliation job during market hours. Peak spiky traffic - we need predictable p95 latencies under 300ms and ability to absorb short spikes up to 3x baseline for 10-15 minutes.
[00:50] Diego: Understood; are you currently serving models on-prem or cloud?
[00:54] Amit: Mostly AWS -- EKS + some EC2 GPU instances. We eval'd self-hosting but ops cost was high, and we use OpenAI for prototyping. For production we want isolation and data controls.
[01:06] Samantha: Perfect, that maps to customers we see moving to Redwood Dedicated. Quick quals: regulatory constraints, data residency, and procurement timeline?
[01:14] Karen: We're regulated (bank) so SOC2/ISO requirements, KMS integration, audit logs, and SSO (SAML) are musts. Timeline is Q2 pilot then decision by end of Q2.
[01:26] Lena: Also need ability to have private control plane or at least VPC peering — no egress of PII outside our VPC.
[01:35] Diego: Redwood Dedicated supports customer VPC peering and we offer a Private deployment option if you need an isolated control plane. For Dedicated we can provision a reserved GPU pool in your AWS account or in a Redwood-managed private environment depending on contract.
[01:51] Amit: Can you clarify reserved GPUs in our account vs Redwood-managed? We care about isolation and our security team prefers resources in our AWS.
[01:59] Diego: Sure. Two common models: 1) Dedicated in customer VPC: we ship an AMI/container spec and orchestrate within your account — you own the network boundary, KMS keys, etc. 2) Redwood-hosted Dedicated: we provide a logically isolated pool (single-tenant) managed by Redwood but with private networking & contractual controls. Both give isolation but the first gives you full infra ownership.
[02:22] Karen: What's the typical GEM — I mean, what's the typical size customers commit to?
[02:29] Samantha: Typical finance customers start with 4-8 GPUs for pilots, then 16-32 for production depending on model size. For e.g., Llama-scale variants or a 7B model at q4 quant runs differently than a 70B model.
[02:43] Diego: Exactly — baseline depends on model choice, q-scaling, token rates. For your latency target (p95 <300ms) and spikes, we usually recommend reserving capacity for baseline plus a burst strategy that can auto-burst to a higher tier or fall back to a compatible model.
[02:58] Amit: How fast can the burst happen? We can't have long warmups during market opens.
[03:03] Diego: We support two forms: immediate burst from a reserved pool (if carved-in capacity exists) — that's instant; and warm-up scale which can add nodes in minutes depending on hardware allocation. For instant short spikes we recommend keeping a small headroom in the reserved pool or using a burst buffer — short lived nodes kept warm.
[03:19] Lena: What's the cost tradeoff of keeping warm nodes vs autoscaling?
[03:23] Samantha: Warm nodes cost more idle, obviously, but cost can be optimized with scheduling (only warm during market windows) and with smaller GPU types for bursts. Redwood Optimize also suggests batching and KV caching to reduce token costs so effective cost can be lower than raw GPU idle cost.
[03:39] Karen: Batching and KV caching — will that change inference latency unpredictably? For client flows we need consistency.
[03:45] Diego: Batching is adaptive — we can set latency SLOs so batching won't exceed your latency thresholds; continuous batching is workload-aware. KV cache is used for prefix reuse — it usually reduces latency for repeated contexts. We can tune aggressiveness per route.
[03:59] Amit: On the hardware side, what GPU types do you recommend? We have access to p4d and g5 series.
[04:05] Diego: p4d/Trn scale are great for latency-sensitive high perf; g5 and a10g are cost-effective. For 7B-style models, 1-2 x a10g per replica often suffices; for 70B you'll need multi-GPU setups (sharded). We will propose a cost/latency tradeoff table in the follow-up.
[04:23] Karen: For audits we need detailed logs of who called what and cryptographic proof of data handling — can Redwood integrate with our KMS and export audit logs?
[04:31] Samantha: Yes — we integrate with AWS KMS/HSM, provide audit logs (per-request metadata), and retain logs for configurable retention windows. We can also support SAML SSO and RBAC for token scoping.
[04:43] Lena: Do logs ever contain request payloads? We need to opt-out and ensure PII never leaves our control plane.
[04:50] Diego: By default we capture metadata (timestamps, model, latency, tokens). You can configure log redaction and retention; for Dedicated in-customer VPC, logs stay in your account.
[05:00] Amit: Ok good. Next, about scaling: how does rolling upgrades and model pinning work? We can't have sudden regression in outputs during trading hours.
[05:08] Diego: We support model pinning per route and staged rollouts (canary/A-B). Rolling upgrades won't affect pinned routes. You can also configure automatic fallback to a validated variant if a new model fails quality checks.
[05:19] Karen: What about SLOs/SLA — do you offer SLAs for Dedicated?
[05:23] Samantha: Yes we have SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers for Dedicated with reserved commits. SLA details are in the contract; higher commits get tighter SLAs.
[05:33] Amit: On burst caps — can we set hard limits so we don't overspend on a bad day?
[05:38] Diego: Absolutely — we have budget guardrails and per-customer burst caps, as well as tokens/spend alerts. Also routing policies can prefer cheaper model variants once cost thresholds hit.
[05:50] Karen: Great. Real quick, how would you size for our expected load — we have baseline 200 requests/min, avg 120 tokens per request, p95 target 300ms.
[05:59] Diego: Quick math — that's about 24k tokens/min baseline. Assuming model A (7B q4) with throughput approx 15k tokens/min per GPU depending on sequence length, you'd need 2 GPUs baseline with some headroom so 3 recommended. For spikes to 3x, we'd want either 2 extra burst GPUs or a burst pool. We'll formalize this in the benchmark plan.
[06:20] Amit: That matches our back of envelope. For internal procurement we need estimated monthly cost for 3 reserved GPUs with burst buffer and support.
[06:28] Samantha: We'll send pricing bands for 3/6/12/24 month commits plus burst pricing. Also include Redwood Optimize discounts if you allow quantized models.
[06:39] Lena: Security deep-dive — we'll need architecture docs, penetration test reports, and SOC2 attestation.
[06:45] Samantha: We'll attach security pack and SOC2 report; can set up a technical security call next week.
[06:52] Karen: For benchmarks — we'd prefer Redwood to run a benchmark in our account with sample payloads. Is that supported?
[06:58] Diego: Yes; we can run benchmark within your VPC (with proper access) or we can run a simulated benchmark in Redwood-managed infra. For most customers we prefer in-customer runs to measure network egress and real latencies.
[07:10] Amit: What about model sizes — we run a proprietary 13B fine-tuned model. Can you support custom model images?
[07:16] Diego: Yes, we support onboarding custom models, provide container spec for model artifacts, and handle sharding/compilation for performance. We'll need the model format and weights access.
[07:27] Samantha: Quick interruption — anyone on the call references legal or procurement constraints other than banking regs?
[07:33] Karen: Standard procurement; we'll need vendor risk assessment and contract review. Our procurement lead will engage after we see pricing.
[07:40] Diego: Noted. A couple technical Qs from Diego to Karen/Amit: are your requests mostly stateless short prompts, or do you have long context sessions?
[07:49] Amit: Mixed — client support short prompts, but also multi-step reconciliation flows with long contexts up to 4k tokens.
[07:56] Diego: Good to know — long contexts favor GPUs with larger memory and may influence batch sizing. We'll include variants in the plan.
[08:04] Karen: Any multitenancy concerns? We must ensure strict isolation per internal business unit.
[08:09] Diego: Dedicated gives you tenant-level isolation; routes can be scoped per BU and RBAC applied. If you need per-BU VPC separation that's possible but increases infra overhead.
[08:20] Amit: On observability — can we get per-route token level cost breakdowns?
[08:24] Samantha: Absolutely, that's in Redwood Console — token-level cost, latency breakdowns, error rates, and per-model dashboards. We'll share screenshots in the follow-up.
[08:34] Lena: Regarding encryption in transit and at rest — we must ensure TLS 1.2+ and keys under our KMS.
[08:40] Diego: We support TLS 1.2/1.3 and KMS integrations; for customer-hosted deployment, keys remain in your account.
[08:47] Karen: Ok, let's talk about a potential pilot: timeframe and success criteria.
[08:52] Samantha: Pilot cadence we recommend 4-6 weeks: week 1 provisioning + onboarding, week 2 model/load validation, week 3 benchmark run, week 4 final tuning and SLA proposal. Success criteria? p95 <300ms on baseline, ability to handle 3x spikes for up to 15 minutes without >5% error rate, and audit/security sign-off.
[09:11] Amit: That sounds reasonable. Procurement wants a price range and an MOU.
[09:16] Samantha: We'll send MOU and pricing bands.
[09:19] Diego: One more technical note — for burst strategy we can recommend keeping 1 warm node per 2 baseline GPUs and using faster GPUs for bursts to reduce warmup costs. Also we can use model variants (quantized) as fallback during extreme load.
[09:34] Karen: How do you validate quality when falling back to a quantized variant? We can't accept large regressions.
[09:40] Diego: We run evals on your prompt set (we'll need a sample prompt corpus) and define quality thresholds. Fallback only triggered if variant passes threshold. We also keep canary traffic to validate.
[09:54] Amit: Sounds good. A quick question on billing: is burst billed at same rate or different?
[09:59] Samantha: Burst billing can be different — typically short burst rates are higher; committed reserved capacity gets discounted rates. We'll show effective TCO across commit lengths.
[10:09] Karen: For procurement, include indemnification and data handling clauses.
[10:13] Samantha: Will do.
[10:16] Diego: Any other technical blockers we should know about?
[10:19] Lena: A couple: we may require on-prem options for some workloads later; also need to verify compatibility with our HSM.
[10:27] Diego: Redwood Private supports on-prem deployment and HSM/KMS integrations; we'll include a sketch of the architecture in the security pack.
[10:35] Karen: Ok let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[10:38] Samantha: Recap: Redwood to send pricing bands and MOU (Samantha), Diego to propose benchmark plan and sizing with GPU recommendations, customer to share telemetry and sample prompts. Security deep-dive scheduled next week. Pilot timeline proposed 4-6 weeks.
[10:52] Amit: Agreed. Any open questions?
[10:56] Lena: No, that's all from security for now.
[10:58] Samantha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with documents and a calendar invite for the security call.
[11:03] Karen: Thanks, bye.
